background.definition: Primary cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is a malignant tumor that may arise from the keratinizing cells of the epidermis or its appendages. It is locally invasive and has the potential to metastasize to other organs of the body. It is commonly seen in individuals older than 50 years of age and on sun-exposed areas.

list.listitem: Varies depending on areas with higher incidence of sun exposure.
Age-adjusted incidence among whites is 100 to 150 per 100,000 persons/year.

A more recent British study found the highest rates of non-melanoma skin cancer in Australia (over 1000/100,000/year), the lowest in Africa (<1/100,000/year). In the UK, the rate was 22.6/100,000/year.
Higher in individuals older than 75 years of age; occurs 2 to 3 times more commonly in men than in women.
Cutaneous SCC is second only to basal cell carcinoma (BCC) in frequency of skin cancer occurrence.
Although the etiology is not truly understood, several factors are thought to contribute to occurrence.
Ultraviolet exposure (UVB more than UVA) is thought to be most important.
Indoor tanning slightly increases the risk of non-melanoma skin cancers, including squamous cell cancer (RR 1.7, 95% CI 1.3-2.2).
Occupational exposure is a risk factor (odds ratio [OR] 1.8).
See below for Risk Factors.
Arises in epidermal keratinocytes.
Patients with actinic keratosis and Bowen's disease are at higher risk of developing SCC.
SCC of the skin and mucus membranes is capable of metastatic spread, most commonly to the lungs.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Exposure to sunlight and ultraviolet radiation
Fair complexion with light blue or green eyes
History of tendency to burn instead of tan
History of skin lesions such as actinic keratosis, Bowen's disease, and erythroplasia of Queyrat

list.listitem: Individuals with prior history of nonmelanoma skin cancer are at higher risk. B

Daily use of SPF 15 sunscreen offers modest protection against SCC. As noted in an Australian study, 140 people would have to use daily sunscreen for 4.5 years to prevent 1 possible case of skin SCC. B

The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) concluded in 2023 that the evidence is still insufficient to recommend for or against routine screening for skin cancer using a total body skin examination for the early detection of cutaneous melanoma, BCC, or skin SCC.

The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) concludes that the evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against routine screening for skin cancer using a total body skin examination for the early detection of cutaneous melanoma, BCC, or skin SCC.

Canadian evidence-based guidelines from the Program in Evidence-Based Care recommend screening stratified by risk (very high, high, or normal), although they acknowledge a lack of RCTs and generally poor quality of evidence.

Very high risk of skin cancer: offer total body examinations twice per year and train patients to do monthly skin examinations. Also, counsel patients regarding skin cancer prevention and self-examination. Patients who have any of the following risk factors are considered at very high risk: (1) immunosuppressive therapy, (2) prior history of skin cancer, (3) two or more relatives with melanoma, (4) greater than five atypical dysplastic nevi or 100 nevi in total, (5) more than 250 treatments with PUVA, and (6) radiation therapy for cancer as a child.

High risk of skin cancer: these individuals have two or more of the following: (1) first-degree relative with melanoma, (2) 50 to 100 nevi, (3) naturally blond or red hair color, (4) freckling tendency, (5) radiation therapy as an adult, and (6) skin that tends to burn easily and tans poorly. These individuals should be instructed on skin self-examination and skin cancer prevention. Patients should be instructed to perform monthly skin self-examinations and have a yearly total skin examination.
Normal risk: routine skin examinations and self-examination counseling are not recommended for the general population not included in the high-risk categories described above.

Daily use of SPF 15 sunscreen offers modest protection against SCC. A systematic review performed by the USPSTF found that behavioral interventions focused on the effect of sun exposure on appearance can reduce the use of tanning and UV exposure.

One industry-sponsored RCT of 240 persons compared celecoxib 200 mg/day with placebo and found a decreased risk of nonmelanoma skin cancer, but no difference in actinic keratoses after 11 months. Further research is needed to confirm this finding before recommending this as an option for prevention.
In an Australian study, 140 people would have to use daily sunscreen for 4.5 years to prevent one possible case of skin SCC.
Use appropriate sun-avoidance measures, such as protective clothing, avoiding midday sun, and avoiding tanning devices.

In patients with a history of two previous non-melanoma skin cancers, nicontinamide (vitamin B3) 500 mg twice daily reduced the risk of subsequent non-melanoma skin cancer somewhat (0.5 vs 0.7 squamous cell cancers, p = 0.05, and 1.8 vs 2.4 basal cell cancers, p = 0.02).
Biopsy any growing or ulcerated lesion that does not heal, bleeds easily, or steadily grows in a sun-exposed area or a mucus membrane. C
SCC may appear to be an indurated nodular or crusted growth that may ulcerate. A nonhealing ulcer without keratinization can be an SCC. C
Common areas for SCC include the lower lip, the nose, the rim of the ears, and the arms (all sun-exposed areas). C
Bowen's disease is SCC in situ and appears like a milder version of invasive SCC. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Variable, but suspect with lesion that does not heal, bleeds easily, and grows; can be a waxy nodule, "scar-like" lesion, umbilicated nodule, or crusty lesion
Solitary nodule with central keratin-filled crater, which grows rapidly and may spontaneously involute
Usually nodular and red and may be ulcerated on sun-exposed areas
May be scaly, ulcerated, erythematous plaques, typically on sun-exposed areas; may also occur on mucous membranes; it is a type of SCC in situ

Differential.Differential_Name: can be a pigmented nodule/macule devoid of surrounding pigmentation
Differential.Differential_Features: Can be a pigmented nodule/macule devoid of surrounding pigmentation
SCC of the extremities found in chronic skin ulcers or burn scars
SCC in situ on the penis or vulva related to human papillomavirus infection

list.listitem: A shave biopsy is usually adequate to make the diagnosis of most SCCs. If there is much keratin on top, a deeper shave may be needed.
A punch biopsy may be better for lesions that are pigmented or appear to be deeper.

The histology report should include the following: pathological pattern; cell morphology; degree of differentiation; histological grade; depth; level of dermal invasion; and presence or absence of perineural, vascular, or lymphatic invasion.

Suspect SCC in patients with a lesion (particularly in a sun-exposed area) that does not heal, bleeds easily, or steadily grows, or nodular or crusted growth that may ulcerate. A nonhealing ulcer without keratinization can be a SCC.
Common areas for SCC include the lower lip, the nose, the rim of the ears, and the arms.
Surgical biopsy is needed to make the diagnosis with any suspicious lesion.

Lesions greater than 2 cm in diameter or greater than 6 mm in thickness should be considered high risk for metastasis. European guidelines recommend imaging (e.g. ultrasound of the regional lymph nodes, MRI, PET-CT, or CT) for staging in these patients.

Surgical resection for definitive treatment of SCC should include margins of 4 to 6 mm, using 6-mm margins for larger tumors, high-risk tumors, tumors extending into the subcutaneous tissue, and tumors in high-risk locations (ear, lip, scalp, eyelids, and nose).A

Consider Mohs surgery, which has the highest cure rates, in the surgical treatment of high-risk SCC, particularly at difficult sites where wide surgical margins may be technically difficult to achieve without functional or cosmetic impairment (ear, lip, nose, and around the eye).B
Curettage with electrodesiccation has excellent cure rates in several series for small (<1 cm), well-differentiated, primary, slow-growing tumors arising on sun-exposed sites. C
Consider systemic adjuvant therapy with a PD-1 inhibitor (e.g. emiplimab, pembrolizumab) for advanced or metastatic cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. B
Invasive SCC should be treated surgically. SCC in situ (Bowen's disease) may be treated with topical medications.
A single RCT (n = 65) found no additional benefit of adding 13-cis -retinoic acid and interferon for patients with aggressive squamous cell cancers.

5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) may be considered for large SCC in situ lesions, especially at potentially poor healing sites, and has been used for "control" rather than cure in some patients with multiple lesions.

Intralesional chemotherapy with 5-FU, interferon, bleomycin, and other agents has not been well studied. The literature is largely limited to case series. Interferon may be an option for patients with SCC who cannot undergo excision. An observational study found an 87% clearance rate for intralesional 5-FU.

Topical imiquimod may be used for SCC in situ, especially for larger lesions or difficult/poorly healing sites. However, it is costly and is currently unlicensed for this indication, and the optimum regimen is not known.

Topical photodynamic therapy has been shown to be equivalent or superior to cryotherapy and 5-FU for SCC in situ, either in efficacy and/or in healing, in RCTs. Consider for lesions that are large, on the lower leg, or at otherwise difficult sites. It is costly.
There are no randomized trials of treatment for squamous cell carcinoma of the conjunctiva in HIV positive patients.
Oral nicotinamide 500 mg BD for 12 months was safe and effective in reducing new NMSC by 23% in high risk patients.

Cemiplimab and pembrolizumab (PD-1 inhibitors) have been recommended for advanced or metastatic cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma based on observational studies. A trial randomized 415 patients with squamous cell carcinoma at high risk of recurrence to cemiplimab or placebo. After 2 years of follow-up, disease-free survival was higher with cemiplimab (87% vs 64%, p < .001, NNT = 4).
Surgical resection for definitive treatment of SCC should include 4 to 6-mm margins, depending on the type of lesion. RCTs of surgery compared with other treatments are lacking, though.

A 4-mm margin should be adequate for well-defined, low-risk tumors, <2 cm in diameter, such margins are expected to remove the primary tumor mass completely in 95% of cases. A 6-mm margin is recommended for larger tumors, high-risk tumors, tumors extending into the subcutaneous tissue, and tumors in high-risk locations (ear, lip, scalp, eyelids, and nose).

Mohs surgery provides precise definition and excision of primary tumor to reduce errors that may arise owing to clinically invisible tumor extension. Consider it in the surgical treatment of high-risk SCC, particularly at difficult sites where wide surgical margins may be technically difficult to achieve without functional or cosmetic impairment (ear, lip, nose, and around the eye). Mohs surgery should provide the highest cure rates (as it does in BCC). A recent US joint specialty guideline identifies 143 different squamous cell carcinoma scenarios, with MOHS deemed appropriate in 102 of them, uncertain in 7, and inappropriate in 34.

A cohort study using propensity score matching for 216 patients with high stage squamous cell carcinoma to compare MOHS with wide local excision (WLE) found higher rates of local recurrence, nodal metastasis or any recurrence compared with WLE.

European guidelines (2020) do not recommend sentinel lymph node biopsy. However, lymph node dissection should be performed when there is evidence of regional nodal involvment. Patients with positive margins should undergo re-excision.

Curettage with electrodesiccation has excellent cure rates in several series for small (<1 cm), well-differentiated, primary, slow-growing tumors arising on sun-exposed sites. Cure rates are higher in experienced hands. The experienced clinician undertaking curettage can detect tumor tissue by its soft consistency. Electrodesiccation is applied to the curetted wound, and the curettage-cautery cycle is then repeated twice.

Cryosurgery has shown good short-term cure rates for small, histologically confirmed SCC treated with experienced hands. Cryosurgery, as well as curettage with electrodesiccation, is not appropriate for locally recurrent disease.
A Cochrane review identified three studies of surgical therapy for SCC of the vulva. The better quality studies support radical local excision for early stage vulvar carcinoma.

A systematic review of 110 studies reporting on 21,569 squamous cell carcinomas found that the proportion of incomplete excisions was 9.4% overall, and was 4.7% for dermatologists, 8.2% for plastic surgeons, and 18.9% for GPs.
Beta carotene at a dose of 50 mg every other day does not reduce the risk of SCC of the skin.

Radiation therapy alone offers short- and long-term cure rates for SCC that are comparable to those with other treatments. It is recommended for lesions arising on the lip, nasal vestibule (and sometimes the outside of the nose), and ear. Certain very advanced tumors, when surgical morbidity would be high, may be treated by radiotherapy. However, a systematic review of low quality mostly observational retrospective studies found no clear evidence to support a benefit of surgery plus radiation over surgery alone.
A systematic review found 3 observational studies with 214 squamous cell carcinomas treated with CO2 laser, with a 22% recurrence rate (95% CI 5%-61%).

With regards to non-excisional treatments, a systematic review of 186 studies with 9336 squamous cell carcinomas and SCC in situ concluded that electrodessication or cryotherapy in combination with curettage are more effective than photodynamic therapy, 5-fluorouracil or imiquimod.
Appropriate consultation is necessary (surgical, oncology, and radiation) for metastatic disease.
Monitor for wound infection immediately after surgery.

For patients with metastatic or locally advanced SCC, anti-PD-1 antibodies are recommended as first-line therapy by European guidelines if patients are not candidates for surgery or radiation therapy. Cetuximab is second line therapy combined with chemotherapy or radiation therapy.

A small RCT randomized 52 patients with locally advanced SCC of the head or neck to everolimus or placebo. There was a significant improvement in progression free survival for P16-negative patients and in TP53-mutated patients (HR 0.24, 95% CI 0.06-0.95).

A Phase 2 study gave 79 patients cemiplimab, up to 4 doses every 3 weeks prior to surgery with curative intent for Stage II to IV squamous cell carcinoma. A complete response was seen in 51% of patients (95% CI 39% to 62%) and a major response in 13% (95% CI 6% to 22%). About half of patients in this study had stage 3 disease and only 2 had metastates. Fatigue, rash, and diarrhea were common adverse effects.
SCC usually has a good prognosis for primary lesions in sun-exposed areas. B

There is a poor prognosis for patients with metastatic disease; 10-year survival rates for patients with regional lymphadenopathy and distant metastasis are less than 20% and less than 10%, respectively. B
Locally destructive, with potential for metastasis if untreated.
SCC has a worse prognosis with larger, deeper, less well-differentiated tumors.

A meta-analysis of 129 studies with 137,449 patients concluded that tumor invasion beyond the subcutaneous fat was associated with local recurrence (RR 9.1, 95% CI 2.8 - 29.2) and disease specific mortality (10.4, 95% CI 3.0-36.3). The risk of metastasis was associated with perineural invasion (RR 5.0; 95%CI 2.3-11.1).

The likelihood of metastasis is low (<4%). It has a higher likelihood of metastasis when it appears on non-sun-exposed sites or the lip or ear. Immunosuppressed hosts and tumors with perineural invasion also carry a higher risk of metastasis.
A meta-analysis found a 3-year risk of recurrence of SCC after an initial SCC of 18% (range 9%-23%). It was 6% (range 1%-19%) following an initial BCC.
Radiation therapy: 85% to 95% cure rates for T1 lesions.
Electrodesiccation and curettage: 5-year cure rates for small SCCs possibly as high as 96% to 99%.

Mohs surgery: micrographic surgical treatment for primary SCC (except those located on the lips and ears) has a 5-year cure rate of 96.9%. For recurrent tumors, Mohs surgery has a 5-year cure rate of 90% to 93.3% compared with 76.7% treated by standard excision.
Lymph node involvement: 30% to 40% 5-year cure rate for combined lymph node dissection and radiation in individuals with lymph node involvement.
The TP53 mutation is associated with worse overall (HR 1.75, 95% CI 1.45-2.10) and disease-specific survival (HR 4.2, 95% CI 1.2-15.1) in patients with head and neck cancer.
Usual recommendation for follow-up in patients with SCC is for a skin examination every month for 3 months, then at 6 months after treatment, and yearly thereafter.
